However, PAA is significantly more expensive than conventional sodium hypochlorite. Thus, precision dose control is key to minimizing cost and ecological impacts. Unfortunately, PAA is difficult to model at full-scale. For example, the Metro Water Recovery Robert W. Hite Treatment Facility (RWHTF) has found both the monitoring and optimization of PAA difficult; such that excessive disinfectant dosing is common. Data-driven models are needed to better understand and quantify real-time disinfection performance and realize chemical reductions. 5.3.2 Define the Problem PAA dosing is not as straightforward as using a set initial PAA concentration to achieve a required log removal of E. coli. Rather, PAA is currently controlled based on the estimated CT, which can be calculated by integrating PAA concentration over hydraulic retention time. PAA concentration in secondary treated wastewaters follows a first order decay model. The required CT is then determined by a second model (double exponential mechanistic model) which explains the relationship between CT and E. coli log inactivation. Finally, the required log inactivation is calculated from the influent E. coli concentration and the discharge limit. However, there are complications to how the estimations made at each step influence the final PAA dose calculation. This leads to significant error and results in a very large safety factor needing to be applied in order to guarantee the E. coli discharge limit is met. Influent E. coli is measured using a grab sample immediately upstream of the PAA dosing point and requires 24-hours for laboratory analysis. To estimate the current influent E. coli, Metro uses a running 3-day average of previous influent E. coli measurements. The calculated log removal is then used with historical CT data to fit a mechanistic model, but it appears that CT is not the only factor that influences E. coli log removal (Figure 5-30). Once the required CT is established, PAA dose can be calculated using previously measured first-order decay parameters and an online analyzer. A PAA analyzer located approximately 10 minutes downstream of the dosing point during average flow conditions adjusts for the initial oxidative demand of PAA (i.e., difference between initial PAA dose and the actual initial concentration) and the first-order decay rate (k) is measured quarterly in the lab. However, k is not as constant as previously assumed (Figure 5-31). Figure 5-31.
